summary: Wilde called him one of 'my dear Neapolitans' and said he missed him after the group went home. The whole of the record is one sentence in a letter to his publisher, in which he weighs a waiter in Paris against him and finds the waiter no consolation.

sources.quote: Is there any chance of your being in Paris? My dear Neapolitans have returned to Naples and I miss that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb. A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick, occasionally serves me drinks at the Café d'Égypte, but he does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris - three months before his death. The same sentence introduces the Café d'Égypte waiter, who has his own entry; the two are different men, and the sentence turns on the contrast between them.
sources.supports: The association and its ending, in Wilde's own words, and the terms he describes him in.
sources.citation_provenance: PDF p. 1242. 'Café d'Égypte' carries its accents in the printed text. The letter is incomplete and descends from a printed memoir and a saleroom catalogue rather than a manuscript - see the editors' footnote 1 on the same page. The same letter as the Café d'Égypte passage, and the same sale: note 1 corrects Spencer's text from the American Art Association catalogue of 1 February 1928.
